DesiredGainR 0.3.0 — Technical Audit

Source: AUDIT-2026-07-30.md

Date: 2026-07-30. Scope: full package tree (R/, man/, tests/, vignettes/, inst/, .github/, DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, README, NEWS, _pkgdown.yml). Audience assumed: quantitative geneticists and breeders.

Note: add ^AUDIT-.*\.md$ to .Rbuildignore so this file does not enter the package tarball.

Status after the 0.3.1 compatibility pass

Addressed, with no argument, function, result-element or column name renamed or removed: §3.3 (gain denominator), §3.4 (ρ²), §3.5 (Γ centring — now warns), §3.9 (constants documented), §3.10 (tie-breaking), and, from §4, the RNG state leak, citEntry(), the DESCRIPTION fields, duplicated globalVariables(), the loop-invariant recomputation, and the missing run_dgsi() examples. §3.1 is documented rather than changed, because changing the interpretation of dg would silently alter every existing caller’s target.

Still open and deliberately deferred: §3.2 (closed-form expected response), §3.6 (uncertainty propagation), §3.7/§3.8 (example data and examples deriving G from phenotypes), §4 predict()/print()/summary(), §5 remaining test gaps, and all of §6.

1. Overall assessment

The package is well above the average R package on discipline: input validation, provenance tracking, refusal to silently substitute a prediction covariance for a genetic covariance, and explicit separation of desired gains from economic weights. That posture is the package’s main asset and it is unusual in this domain.

The gap is between that posture and the statistical content. Three of the reported quantities are internally inconsistent or scale-ambiguous, the DGSI optimiser targets a quantity that is not the classical expected genetic response, uncertainty in the estimated G/Γ is nowhere propagated, and the index families a selection-index specialist would look for first (restricted, predetermined-proportional-gain, Smith–Hazel/LGSI baselines) are absent. As it stands the package is a solid, honest scoring engine; it is not yet a reference implementation an expert panel would adopt without changes.

2. Strengths

Scientific hygiene. run_dgsi() refuses to run without G; run_qgsi() refuses to fabricate W; estimate_genetic_covariance() labels its estimand rather than calling every covariance “genetic”; accuracy and MSPE are withheld unless true_G is supplied; observed_selection_differential is explicitly not called realised gain. This is exactly the discipline that is usually missing in breeding-index code, and it is enforced in code, not only in prose.

Provenance and auditability. covariance_provenance, transformation, missing_data, assumptions, and the equation references travel with the result object. A reviewer can reconstruct what was done from the fitted object alone.

Numerical care. Symmetrisation of user matrices, relative-tolerance symmetry and PSD checks, spectral Moore–Penrose inverse with reported rank for rank-deficient Φ, ridge terms on both solves, and rejection of negative model variances. The .dgr_qg_symmetric_matrix() / .dgr_check_psd() helpers are correct and consistently applied.

Correct core algebra where it is implemented. The Pesek–Baker coefficient b = P⁻¹G(GᵀP⁻¹G)⁻¹d is correctly formed; the QGSI score, E(I)=tr(WΓ), w'Γw, and 2tr(WΓWΓ) are correct for Gaussian γ; the two Γ estimators match the cited equations including the divisor g.

Stability reporting. Replicate diagnostics, plateau detection, Spearman rank-correlation across replicates, coefficient CV, and Jaccard selected-set agreement are more than most index packages report, and automatic best-replicate selection removes a manual cherry-picking step.

Lightweight dependencies. data.table, stats, utils only. Installs anywhere, no compilation, no dependency drift risk.

Infrastructure basics present. MIT licence with LICENSE file, roxygen docs, testthat 3e, R-CMD-check on three OSes, pkgdown site with favicons, issue templates, NEWS.md, CITATION, CITATION.cff, logo.

3. Weaknesses — correctness and statistics (highest priority)

3.1 DGSI: dg units are ambiguous and probably misinterpreted by users

run_dgsi() documents dg as “desired gains in the analysis scale”, and scale_traits defaults to FALSE, so X stays in raw trait units. But realised_response() divides by the candidate-column SD:

base_sd <- apply(matrix, 2L, stats::sd)
response <- (colMeans(matrix[keep, ]) - colMeans(matrix)) / base_sd

So the quantity compared with dg is always in candidate-SD units. A breeder who writes dg = c(YLD = 1.5) meaning 1.5 t/ha silently gets a target of 1.5 phenotypic SD. inst/examples/demo_pipeline.R does exactly this. Either rename the argument (dg_sd), or transform dg by base_sd internally, or require scale_traits = TRUE when dg is on the SD scale. Document the convention in the @param text, not only in the vignette.

3.2 DGSI optimises an empirical selection differential, not expected genetic response

The classical desired-gain index has a closed-form guarantee: with b = P⁻¹G(GᵀP⁻¹G)⁻¹d, the expected genetic response R = i·Gb/√(bᵀPb) is proportional to d. The package computes b from that formula but then scores it against the realised standardised mean shift of the top-n_select candidates, and hill-climbs over d. That is a different estimand, it is a step function of b (hence the need for a stochastic search), and it is evaluated on the same candidates that are then selected.

Consequences: - The closed-form solution is never reported as a reference point. Add it. - R = i·Gb/√(bᵀPb), the index accuracy ρ_HI, and the achieved-vs-desired gain ratio are never returned. These are the numbers a breeder is asked for. - Best-of-n_rep selection on the training candidates is optimistically biased. The validation_data slot evaluates the winner but does not participate in choosing it. Consider selecting the replicate on held-out data, or reporting the optimism gap. - Results depend on n_rep: increasing it changes the answer, which is awkward for a package that advertises auditability.

3.3 QGSI: expected per-trait gain uses the wrong index SD

expected_gain <- selection_intensity * Gamma %*% weights / sqrt(linear_variance)

linear_variance is wᵀΓw. But expected_net_merit_response two lines earlier uses sqrt(index_variance) = sqrt(wᵀΓw + 2tr(WΓWΓ)). The regression of γ on I gives R_γ = i·Cov(γ, I)/σ_I, and σ_I is the total index SD. Dividing by the linear part alone inflates every per-trait gain whenever W ≠ 0 — that is, in every genuine QGSI run. This looks like the LGSI formula carried over unchanged.

tests/testthat/test-qgsi-theory.R:78 asserts the current formula, so the test suite locks the behaviour in rather than checking it. Verify against Supplementary Eq. 16 of Cerón-Rojas et al. (2026) and, whichever way it resolves, add a comment in the code stating which σ the equation uses.

3.4 QGSI: squared accuracy ignores the covariance it just computed

merit_index_covariance <- linear_variance + 2*tr(W %*% Gamma %*% W %*% true_G)
...
accuracy_squared <- index_variance / merit_variance

ρ² = Cov(H,I)² / (Var(I)·Var(H)). The code returns Var(I)/Var(H), which equals ρ² only when Cov(H,I) = Var(I) — i.e. only when I is the optimal (MSPE-minimising) predictor of H. The package accepts arbitrary user-supplied w and W, so that identity generally fails, and the code computes merit_index_covariance explicitly, confirming it is not assumed equal. Either use the general formula or document and enforce the optimality condition.

Related: the package never states the identification θ = w, D = W (index coefficients equal economic weights) under which the paper’s genomic results hold. That assumption is doing real work and should be explicit, with its conditions.

3.5 QGSI: Γ is centred even when center_traits = FALSE

.dgr_qg_estimate_gamma() starts with X_cov <- sweep(X, 2, colMeans(X), "-") unconditionally. If the user sets center_traits = FALSE (because their weights refer to an uncentred origin — a legitimate choice for a quadratic index, where the origin determines whether curvature means stabilising or disruptive selection), the scores use uncentred γ while Γ, E(I) = tr(WΓ), and all variance formulas use centred γ. The theoretical block then does not describe the index that was actually computed. Either centre consistently, or warn.

3.6 Sampling error in G, P, and Γ is nowhere propagated

Every reported quantity treats the covariance matrices as known constants. In practice G comes from a multi-trait REML fit on tens to a few hundred genotypes and is badly conditioned; index coefficients are notoriously unstable under that noise. For a package whose selling point is auditability, this is the largest scientific omission. Minimum viable additions: bootstrap or delta-method standard errors for b and for the expected gains; a sensitivity analysis that perturbs G within its sampling distribution and reports the resulting rank churn; a bending / shrinkage option (nearPD, Ledoit–Wolf) for non-PSD or ill-conditioned REML output, which the package currently only rejects.

3.7 Degenerate default when ref_data and P are both omitted

With P = NULL and ref_data = NULL, P becomes cov(X_candidates). If G was also derived from the same candidates (as in the README, vignette and demo), P ≈ G, so P⁻¹G ≈ I and the index collapses towards b ∝ d. All three shipped examples do this. At minimum, warn when P and G are numerically close; better, refuse the combination or document it prominently.

3.8 Shipped examples contradict the package’s own doctrine

R/estimate_genetic_covariance.R and both narrative documents state that raw phenotypes cannot identify genetic covariance. Then inst/examples/demo_pipeline.R:9 computes G <- stats::cov(as.matrix(values[, ..traits])) from example_pheno.csv, and README/vignette do the same on rnorm() data. This undercuts the package’s credibility with exactly the audience it targets.

3.9 Magic constants and undocumented objective shape

objective() uses denominator <- pmax(abs(dg), 0.25). The 0.25 floor changes the relative weighting of traits with small desired gains and appears in no documentation. Expose it as an argument or justify it in @details. Similarly, proposal_sd <- sd_scale * pmax(abs(centre), 0.05) hides a second constant.

3.10 Inconsistent tie-breaking

run_qgsi() breaks ties deterministically by candidate ID. run_dgsi() uses order(score[pool], decreasing = TRUE), so ties resolve by row order — results change if the input rows are reordered. Make DGSI match QGSI.

4. Weaknesses — API and software engineering

set.seed() mutates the caller’s RNG. run_dgsi() calls set.seed(as.integer(seed)) and never restores .Random.seed. A package should save and restore it (or use withr::with_seed). This silently changes downstream results in a user’s simulation script.

No methods for desired_gain_index. print, summary, plot (objective trace, coefficient stability, achieved-vs-desired gain), coef, and predict (apply fitted coefficients to a new candidate set) are all absent. predict() in particular is what makes an index reusable across cycles; validation_data only covers fit time.

Pipeline is a lossy pass-through. run_dgsi_qgsi_pipeline() does not expose missing_policy, objective_weights, validation_data, plateau_window, plateau_tolerance, or return_all_reps for DGSI, and renames select_mode = "eligible_top_n" to "trait_thresholds". Two vocabularies for the same concept in one package.

Unsafe default in the pipeline. fallback_to_top_n = TRUE means the pipeline silently ignores the breeder’s eligibility thresholds when nothing qualifies. run_dgsi() defaults to "error". The safe default should win, and in a package built on “nothing happens silently” this one stands out.

debug = TRUE defaults. run_dgsi_qgsi_pipeline() and run_qgsi_desired_gain() default to verbose; run_dgsi()/run_qgsi() do not. Packages should be quiet by default.

Deprecation mechanics. run_qgsi_desired_gain() uses a bare warning(). Use .Deprecated() or a lifecycle badge so it appears in the docs and in R CMD check output, and give it a removal target in NEWS.

Dead and duplicated code. .validate_square_matrix() and .desiredgainr_z() are defined and never called; .validate_square_matrix() even has a generated man/dot-validate_square_matrix.Rd. globalVariables() is called in both R/globals.R and R/utils_internal.R with overlapping and partly obsolete names (Rank_LinearDGPart, SignSame_DG_QGSI, ..dg_cols_present).

Performance. The search is n_rep × n_iter evaluations (default 20,000), each recomputing X %*% b, a full column-SD pass, colMeans, and a sort of the whole pool. apply(matrix, 2, sd) and colMeans(matrix) are loop-invariant and should be hoisted — that alone is a large win. There is no parallelism over replicates (parallel/future.apply) and no compiled code. On 20k candidates × 15 traits this will be slow enough to discourage use.

inst/CITATION uses citEntry(). Deprecated since R 4.2; modern R CMD check flags it. Switch to bibentry(bibtype = "Manual", ...).

DESCRIPTION issues. Author:/Maintainer: are hand-written alongside Authors@R (redundant, can drift out of sync); no Depends: R (>= 4.1) or similar; no Language: en-GB despite consistent British spelling, which will trip CRAN’s spell check; Config/roxygen2/version: 8.0.0 should be verified against the roxygen2 actually used.

Undocumented example data. inst/extdata/*.csv have no data documentation, no provenance, no units, and no description of YLD/MY/MI/BL/NBL/VHB. The values are uncorrelated standard normals, so G ≈ I and the examples cannot demonstrate the multi-trait behaviour that is the entire point. Replace with a simulated dataset that has a realistic G (documented correlations, heritabilities, trait means and units) or a de-identified real trial.

Missing @examples. run_dgsi(), estimate_genetic_covariance(), and compare_dg_and_qgsi() have none. run_dgsi() is the flagship function.

5. Weaknesses — testing

Five test files, roughly 30 assertions. Untested paths include:

  • run_dgsi(): validation_data, objective_weights, mean_impute and complete_cases policies, scale_traits = TRUE, non-PSD G rejection, empty_eligibility = "fallback_top_n", plateau diagnostics, ref_data distinct from cand_data, lower_is_better sign propagation into P/G.
  • run_qgsi(): reference_gebv_data, scale_traits = TRUE, rank-deficient relationship_matrix (the Moore–Penrose branch is advertised but only the full-rank branch is tested), selection_proportion edge values.
  • run_dgsi_qgsi_pipeline(): mode = "dg" and mode = "qgsi" alone.
  • Both print methods; compare_dg_and_qgsi() legacy-column renaming.

More important than coverage: there are no property tests against known answers. A specialist reviewer will look for (a) a case where the closed-form Pesek–Baker b reproduces d exactly, (b) a Monte-Carlo check that the QGSI Var(I) and E(I) formulas match simulation from a multivariate normal γ, (c) a check that the expected per-trait gain matches the realised gain under simulated truncation selection. Test (c) would have caught §3.3 immediately.

No coverage measurement (covr + codecov workflow), no lint config, and CI tests only release — add oldrel-1 and devel.

6. What is missing (feature gaps for the target audience)

Index families. A package named for desired gains should implement the theory-backed relatives: the restricted index (Kempthorne–Nordskog), the null-restricted / Mallard index, and above all the predetermined proportional-gains index (PPG-LPSI, Tallis 1985; Cerón-Rojas & Crossa), which is the formally justified version of what run_dgsi() approximates by search. Also missing: Smith–Hazel LPSI and the linear genomic index LGSI as baselines — without them the package cannot reproduce the comparisons in the very paper it cites.

Reporting a breeder expects. Expected genetic response per trait with standard errors, correlated response, index accuracy ρ_HI, index heritability, selection differential vs expected gain, and gain per unit time/cycle. The QGSI side has some of this; the DGSI side has almost none.

Diversity and constraint. No coancestry or inbreeding control, no optimal contribution selection, no mate allocation, no per-family or per-group quotas beyond the single eligibility threshold. Real programmes cannot select on gain alone, and this is the most commonly requested feature in comparable tools.

Upstream integration. No adapters for the objects breeders actually hold: sommer::mmer ($sigma, $PevU), ASReml-R (vparameters, predict PEV), lme4/breedR, rrBLUP/BGLR GEBVs, AGHmatrix/ASRgenomics relationship matrices. An as_genetic_covariance() S3 generic over those classes would be the single highest-value addition for adoption, and it fits the package’s provenance philosophy perfectly.

Multi-environment and multi-stage. No GxE handling, no multi-environment index, no multi-stage/two-stage selection, no across-cycle response prediction (Bulmer effect, drift of G).

Elicitation and sensitivity for W. The package correctly refuses to invent W, but then offers the breeder no help constructing it. A vignette (or helper) on translating agronomic and economic objectives into w and W, with a sensitivity/tornado analysis over plausible weight sets, would convert the current refusal from an obstacle into a feature.

Ill-conditioned input handling. Bending / nearest-PD projection, shrinkage estimators for Γ when p is large relative to g, and a condition-number diagnostic. Currently non-PSD input is simply an error, which will send users to ad-hoc fixes outside the package.

Documentation gaps. One vignette only. Worth adding: a real worked case study end-to-end from a REML fit; a “choosing W” vignette; a validation vignette reproducing the published QGSI results; and a methods/theory vignette stating every estimand and the conditions under which each reported number is valid.

Publication and archiving. No CRAN submission artefacts (cran-comments.md), no Zenodo DOI, no JOSS/preprint. For a package meant to be cited by breeders, a versioned DOI and a short methods paper matter more than another feature.

7. Suggested priority order

  1. Resolve §3.3 (per-trait gain denominator) and §3.4 (ρ²) against the published supplementary equations; fix the tests that currently lock them in.
  2. Fix the dg scale ambiguity (§3.1) and add the closed-form expected response i·Gb/√(bᵀPb) and accuracy to the DGSI output (§3.2).
  3. Fix Γ centring consistency (§3.5), RNG state restoration, and tie-breaking.
  4. Replace the example data and rewrite the three examples so they no longer derive G from raw phenotypes (§3.7, §3.8).
  5. Add Monte-Carlo property tests for every theoretical formula.
  6. Add predict(), print(), summary(), plot() for desired_gain_index.
  7. Add uncertainty propagation for G/Γ (bootstrap + sensitivity) (§3.6).
  8. Add the PPG/restricted index family and LPSI/LGSI baselines.
  9. Add upstream adapters (sommer, ASReml-R) and a real worked-example vignette.
  10. Housekeeping: bibentry(), DESCRIPTION cleanup, dead code, CI matrix, coverage.
